definition.text: A chemical reaction in which the oxidation states of the reactants change; short for reduction–oxidation.

facts.text: Oxidation is a loss of electrons, or a rise in oxidation state; reduction is a gain of electrons, or a fall in oxidation state.
The two always happen together and cannot occur independently.
When iron rusts, the iron is oxidized to an oxide while oxygen is reduced by taking up the released electrons.
Respiration, photosynthesis, combustion and the corrosion of metals all run on redox chemistry.
In soils, sediments and water, redox gradients drive the biogeochemical cycling of elements.
Oxidation first meant reacting with oxygen, and reduction the weight lost when ore is heated to extract metal; both were later generalized to electron transfer.
The word redox first appeared in a 1928 article by Leonor Michaelis and Louis B. Flexner.

definition.text: A substance that oxidizes another by taking its electrons, and is itself reduced; also called an oxidant or electron acceptor.

facts.text: Oxidants usually contain elements in high oxidation states, such as permanganate, or are highly electronegative elements such as oxygen and chlorine.
Oxygen is the electron acceptor with the highest redox potential.
In oxidizing soils, oxygen accepts electrons and is reduced to water.

title: Reducing agent

definition.text: A substance that reduces another by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidized; also called a reductant or electron donor.

facts.text: Electropositive metals such as lithium, sodium, magnesium, iron, zinc and aluminium donate electrons readily and are good reducing agents.
A reducing equivalent is whatever transfers the equivalent of one electron, an electron or a hydrogen atom; the term is common in biochemistry.
Underground electron donors include organic matter, hydrogen, methane, reduced sulfur and iron compounds, and ammonium.
Organic matter is the main source of electrons in soil.

notes: Deep biosphere lists donors 'from highest to lowest redox potential' starting with organic matter (S:604107f730f9), yet says organic matter has the most negative redox potential of the donors (S:5883772d0343); the ordering claim was left out.

definition.text: A redox couple is a reducing species and its oxidized form, such as Fe2+/Fe3+; the oxidation and the reduction taken alone are each a half-reaction.

facts.text: In a redox reaction the reductant passes electrons to the oxidant, so the reductant is oxidized and the oxidant reduced.
The oxidizing and reducing agents in a given reaction form a redox pair.
In electrochemical reactions the two half-reactions happen at the same time but in different places.
The terms confuse many: the reagent that is oxidized is called the reducing agent, and the one reduced the oxidizing agent.

definition.text: The equilibrium voltage of a half-reaction under standard conditions, measured against a standard hydrogen electrode; also called its reduction potential.

facts.text: It measures how strongly an oxidizing agent tends to be reduced.
It is zero for hydrogen ions by definition, positive for stronger oxidants such as fluorine (+2.866 V) and negative for weaker ones such as zinc ions (−0.763 V).
A cell's potential is the cathode potential minus the anode potential.
Reduction potential is measured in volts or millivolts.

definition.text: The electron-transfer reactions that underlie many soil processes and properties.

facts.text: Redox potential, expressed as Eh or as pe (the negative log of electron activity, like pH), is a master variable that, with pH, both controls and reflects soil reactions.
Soil chemical reactions involve some combination of proton and electron transfer.
Early theory grew out of flooded soils and paddy rice and shaped later work on redox thermodynamics and root growth.
Later work extended it to heavy metals, soil formation and morphology, organic compounds, wetland delineation, remediation and ways to characterize soil redox status.
Redox acts on soil development, and redoximorphic colour features give critical information for interpreting soils.
Soil microbes organize along electron transport chains, forming electrically conductive biofilms and networks of bacterial nanowires.
Understanding soil redox gradients matters for carbon sequestration, bioremediation, wetland delineation and soil-based microbial fuel cells.

definition.text: The redox reactions on which many essential life processes run, above all respiration and photosynthesis.

facts.text: Aerobic respiration oxidizes substrates such as glucose and reduces oxygen to water.
Photosynthesis reduces carbon dioxide to sugars and oxidizes water to oxygen; it complements respiration but is not simply its reverse.
Living things often store and release energy through redox reactions, relying on the cycling of NAD+ and NADH.

definition.text: Colour patterns in soil from the loss or gain of pigment against the matrix colour, formed by oxidation and reduction of iron or manganese and their movement, or a matrix colour set by ferrous iron.

facts.text: A colour pattern counts as redoximorphic only once the processes that formed it are known or inferred.
Reducing conditions give disrupted colour with complex mottled patterns and points of colour concentration, whereas aerobic conditions give uniform or gradual changes.
As a wet soil dries and oxygen returns, reduced iron can re-oxidize locally into bright yellow-brown mottles.
They provide critical information for soil interpretation.
Classification uses them: Vertisols with aquic conditions and redoximorphic features are Aquerts, and the WRB suffix σ marks permanent saturation without them.
Eh, the voltage measured in a soil, expresses the potential for redoximorphic reactions to occur.
Fluctuating water levels cause alternating oxidation and reduction, producing mottling of red and yellow blotches mixed with gray.
Continuous strong reduction from long-term waterlogging gives gleyed conditions with dark gray to blue to black colors.

title: Redox gradient

definition.text: A series of redox reactions sorted according to redox potential.

facts.text: Redox gradients form in space and time from differences in microbial processes, chemical composition and oxidative potential.
They are driven by oxygen availability, soil hydrology, the chemical species present and microbial activity.
They are typical of waterlogged soils, wetlands, lakes, coastal marshes, contaminant plumes and marine sediments.
The Earth as a whole is oxidizing at the surface and increasingly reducing below it.
They are well understood at large scale, but micro-scale redox in heterogeneous settings needs more research and better measurement.

distinct_from: Redox gradients in water and sediments

title: Redox ladder

definition.text: The order in which redox reactions take place, set by the free energy each redox pair yields.

facts.text: The most energetically favourable reaction sits at the top of the ladder and the least favourable at the bottom.
From oxidizing to reducing the usual sequence is aerobic respiration, denitrification, manganese reduction, iron reduction and sulfate reduction.
For anaerobic respiration the nitrate–nitrogen couple ranks just below oxygen, above manganese, iron, sulfate and finally carbon dioxide–methane.
As oxygen dwindles with depth in sediments, microbial respiration pathways stack in vertical layers.
Thermodynamics alone does not fix where microbes live; ecological and physiological factors also matter.

distinct_from: Redox gradients in water and sediments

title: Redox potential (Eh)

definition.text: The tendency of electrons to pass from an electron donor to an electron acceptor, measured in volts as Eh.

facts.text: Eh is zero for the standard hydrogen electrode couple; positive values mean an oxidizing environment that accepts electrons, negative values a reducing one that donates them.
It can be calculated from half-reactions with the Nernst equation.
Soil Eh generally ranges from −300 to +900 mV; cultivated soils typically sit between +300 and +500 mV.
Plants are generally held to tolerate +300 to +700 mV, and 300 mV separates aerobic from anaerobic conditions in wetland soils.
Eh is closely tied to pH, and higher redox potentials occur at lower pH.
Oxidation state of the species present, pH and the amount of oxygen together control a system's redox potential.
Aerated waters usually show positive potentials, while places short of air, such as submerged soils, swamps and marine sediments, are normally reducing with negative potentials.
Strict aerobes are generally active at positive Eh and strict anaerobes at negative Eh; facultative anaerobes work at negative Eh too when nitrate or sulfate is present.

distinct_from: Redox gradients in water and sediments

title: Measuring redox potential

definition.text: Determining Eh by sampling in the field and analysing in the lab, or by placing an electrode in the soil or water for in situ readings.

facts.text: Soil Eh is read with a platinum electrode relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.
Many samples give fine spatial but poor temporal resolution; fixed electrodes give continuous readings but poor spatial coverage.
Waters, soils and sediments can be highly heterogeneous, which complicates measurement.
Induced-polarization imaging can track redox at high spatial and temporal resolution, though its signal is not yet fully understood.

distinct_from: Redox gradients in water and sediments

title: Reduction in waterlogged soils

definition.text: The shift of a saturated soil from oxidizing to reducing conditions as oxygen runs out and anaerobic microbes take over.

facts.text: Soil Eh depends largely on hydrology: flooding turns soil from oxic to anoxic, and draining and drying restore its starting Eh.
Small anoxic hotspots can develop inside soil pores even when the soil as a whole is not saturated.
Organic matter is the main source of electrons; decomposers consume oxygen as they break it down, lowering Eh.
Flooded above about 5 °C, soil loses its oxygen to microbes within a few days, and nitrate and ferric oxide are then reduced.
At high redox potential iron is deposited as ferric hematite; under low redox conditions ferrous iron builds up and decomposition slows.
Prolonged saturation can dissolve ferric iron minerals that hold phosphorus, releasing it to leaching.

distinct_from: Redox gradients in water and sediments

title: Microbes along redox gradients

definition.text: The layered microbial communities that redox gradients support, and that in turn sharpen those gradients through their respiration.

facts.text: Microbes switch respiration processes, such as methanogenesis or sulfate reduction, to suit local conditions, amplifying the gradient.
Organic pollutants break down fastest at the oxic–anoxic interface, such as the groundwater capillary fringe, where electron donors and acceptors abound.
Cable bacteria, which oxidize sulfide, link zones short of electrons with zones holding a surplus.
Biofilms of metal- or sulfate-reducing bacteria create redox gradients on the micrometre scale.

distinct_from: Redox gradients in water and sediments

title: Redox gradients in water and sediments

definition.text: The redox gradients that form in water columns and in the sediments beneath them.

facts.text: Oxic, suboxic and hypoxic water layers allow different redox reactions, and oxygen minimum zones add to the gradients.
In bottom sediments, gradients arise from differences in minerals, organic matter, structure and sorption.
Slow electron transport and varied pore sizes make bottom sediments highly heterogeneous.

title: Anaerobic respiration

definition.text: Respiration that uses inorganic electron acceptors other than oxygen, such as nitrate, sulfate or sulfur, at the end of the electron transport chain.

facts.text: These acceptors have lower reduction potentials than oxygen, so less energy is released and it is less efficient than aerobic respiration; it differs from fermentation, which passes electrons to organic compounds.
Under a few millimetres of water, heterotrophic bacteria use up the soil's oxygen, forcing a switch to anaerobic respiration.
Even oxygenated soil holds oxygen-free micro-environments, because oxygen gas diffuses slowly.
Anaerobic processes such as denitrification, sulfate reduction and methanogenesis release nitrogen gas, hydrogen sulfide and methane; others change the oxidation state of iron and manganese.
Nitrate respiration (denitrification) is the main route returning fixed nitrogen to the air as N2; sulfate respiration makes hydrogen sulfide, the rotten-egg smell of coastal wetlands.
Aerobic respiration releases carbon dioxide, while anaerobic respiration releases methane.
Because decomposition is anaerobic, wetland soils store large amounts of organic carbon.
Martinus Beijerinck discovered bacterial sulfate reduction, a form of anaerobic respiration.

notes: Gap-fill: article set to the Anaerobic respiration page; earlier soil sentences kept.

title: Methanogenesis

definition.text: The formation of methane by microbes called methanogens, all of them archaea, as the final step in breaking down organic matter where oxygen is absent.

facts.text: In most freshwater wetlands sulfate is scarce, and methanogenesis takes over decomposition only once sulfate is used up.
In sediments, sulfate reducers take most of the hydrogen in upper layers, while methanogens dominate lower down where sulfate is depleted.
Methanogenic archaea in the anaerobic layers of peat combine carbon dioxide and hydrogen gas into methane and water.
Methanotrophs oxidize methane back to carbon dioxide; methane production is typically high in anoxic floodplain, lake and reservoir sediments.
Once every electron acceptor but carbon dioxide is used up, only methanogenesis and fermentation can proceed; without methanogenesis much carbon would pile up as fermentation products.
It is common in flooded rice fields and wetlands, natural methane sources, and needs microbes that prefer low oxygen.
Aerating such soils raises sulfate and nitrate, which cut methane production; in upland soils it is often confined to anoxic microsites inside aerobic bulk soil.
Methane's global warming potential is 25 times that of carbon dioxide, averaged over 100 years.

notes: Gap-fill: article set to the Methanogenesis page and weight raised to Major; earlier wetland and sediment sentences kept.

definition.text: A pollution control technique in which a bioreactor holding living material captures pollutants and breaks them down biologically.

facts.text: Uses include treating wastewater, catching harmful chemicals or silt from surface runoff, and microbial oxidation of air pollutants.
Microorganisms attach to a bed of media such as sand, crushed rock or gravel and grow into a biofilm that degrades the pollutants.
Biofiltration was first introduced in England in 1893 as a trickling filter for wastewater.
Bioswales, constructed and natural wetlands and riparian zones work as biofilters; buildup of biomass can clog the media.

definition.text: A remediation technique that injects strong chemical oxidizers into contaminated soil or groundwater to destroy contaminants where they lie.

facts.text: It treats many organic compounds, including some that resist natural breakdown, and works well on chlorinated solvents and gasoline compounds such as benzene and toluene.
Hydrogen peroxide was first used in 1985, on a formaldehyde spill in Springfield, Massachusetts.
Oxidants are delivered through direct-push rods or injection wells, or by soil mixing and hydraulic fracturing where permeability is low.
Success depends on site lithology, oxidant dose and residence time, competing oxidizable material and contact with the contaminant; rising carbon dioxide signals oxidation.
All the main oxidants are strong and pose serious hazards to the people handling them.

title: ISCO oxidants
article: In situ chemical oxidation#Agents of Oxidization

definition.text: The strong oxidizers used in in situ chemical oxidation, most commonly permanganate, Fenton's reagent, persulfate and ozone.

facts.text: Fenton's reagent, hydrogen peroxide catalysed by iron, and potassium permanganate have been used longest and are still widely used.
Permanganate needs double bonds in its targets and is consumed by non-target organic matter in soil; persulfate, introduced in the late 1990s, avoids these limits.
Fenton's reagent makes hydroxyl radicals but needs lowered pH to keep iron dissolved, so whether field use is truly a Fenton reaction is disputed.
Ozone is about 12 times more soluble than oxygen and, being a gas, is injected from below so its bubbles rise through the contamination.

contested_note: Sources report controversy over whether ISCO with Fenton's reagent, applied at near-neutral pH, is really a Fenton reaction.

definition.text: A flooded field of arable land used to grow semiaquatic crops, above all rice and taro.

facts.text: Paddy farming, still the dominant way to grow rice, began in the Neolithic rice cultures of the Yangtze River basin.
Paddies are a major methane source, estimated at 50 to 100 million tonnes a year, about 10% of global methane emissions.
Draining paddies so the soil aerates interrupts methane production and can boost yield, while ammonium-based fertilizers raise emissions.
Long wet-field cultivation can turn paddy soils into Anthrosols, and early soil redox theory grew out of flooded paddy rice soils.

definition.text: Anaerobic respiration by bacteria and archaea that use a metal, rather than oxygen, as the terminal electron acceptor.

facts.text: Iron and manganese are the metals most used: Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II) and Mn(IV) to Mn(II), and most Fe(III) reducers can also reduce Mn(IV).
Other metals and metalloids can serve too, including vanadium, chromium(VI), molybdenum, cobalt, palladium, gold and mercury.
It happens without oxygen, but the organisms include both strict anaerobes such as the Geobacteraceae and facultative anaerobes such as Shewanella.
In near-neutral soils and sediments iron is held in solid oxidized minerals, so these microbes reduce metals outside the cell, passing electrons out through membrane cytochromes c.
Some reduce minerals at a distance using electron shuttles; humic acids common in soils and sediments can act as such shuttles.
Many Fe(III) minerals can be reduced, including magnetite, hematite, goethite, lepidocrocite, ferrihydrite, smectite, illite and jarosite.
Secondary minerals such as magnetite, siderite, green rust and vivianite can form as by-products of the reduction.

definition.text: A family of green layered iron(II)–iron(III) hydroxides that hold another anion, such as carbonate, chloride or sulfate, between their layers.

facts.text: In nature it occurs as the mineral fougerite, and it is suspected in bluish-green soils formed under alternating redox conditions that turn ochre once exposed to air.
In oxidizing conditions it generally converts to the iron(III) oxyhydroxides goethite and lepidocrocite.
Iron-reducing bacteria such as Shewanella putrefaciens produce it when they reduce ferric oxyhydroxides while oxidizing organic matter, a process thought to occur in soil solutions and aquifers.
Sulfate green rust can reduce nitrate and nitrite to ammonium as its Fe2+ is oxidized to Fe3+.

definition.text: Chemotrophic bacteria that get their energy by oxidizing dissolved iron.

facts.text: They live where oxygen-free water meets an oxygenated setting, turning dissolved iron into an insoluble reddish-brown slime; they need at least 0.3 ppm dissolved oxygen.
Soil microbes feeding on dissolved organic matter, for example from landfill leachate or septic fields, can deoxygenate groundwater and so set the stage for them.
Bog iron ore deposits formed where such groundwater emerged and met atmospheric oxygen.
Some oxidize Fe(II) without oxygen by coupling it to nitrate reduction, a light-independent metabolism found in sediments including paddy soil.

definition.text: The biogeochemical cycle that moves manganese through the atmosphere, water, living things and rocks and soils.

facts.text: Manganese makes up about 0.1% of the Earth's crust and is cycled much like iron, but by distinct redox pathways.
Some bacteria oxidize manganese to insoluble oxides, while others reduce it to soluble Mn2+ in order to use it.
Weathering of regolith and dissolution of bedrock carry manganese into rivers and on to the ocean, where it can form minerals and be buried.
Mining, mineral processing and the burning of fossil fuels are altering the global cycle.
Over half the manganese in ridge soils near iron or steel plants in North America and Europe came from industrial waste and settled airborne particles.

definition.text: The forms and redox behaviour of manganese in soils, where it is a micronutrient whose solubility is set by redox potential and pH.

facts.text: Manganese is a key soil micronutrient, acting as a catalyst in the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II.
Soil fungi oxidize soluble Mn2+ and may reprecipitate it as manganese oxides; much of the soil cycle is biological, though inorganic reactions also oxidize Mn.
As pH rises, manganese speciation becomes less sensitive to pe.
In acidic soils (pH 5) with high pe (above 8), manganese is mostly in reducible forms, and exchangeable and soluble Mn fall sharply as pe rises.

definition.text: Anaerobic archaea that produce methane as a by-product of their energy metabolism.

facts.text: Methanogenesis is their only biochemical pathway for making ATP, and all known methanogens belong to the domain Archaea.
They are common in oxygen-free settings such as wetlands, sediments, rice paddy soil, landfills, wastewater plants and animal guts.
Their oxygen sensitivity varies: methanogenesis is often detected in temporarily oxygenated rice paddy soil, and one wetland and soil species works in anoxic microsites within aerobic soil.
Methanogens grow at a redox potential below −0.3 V.

definition.text: Microorganisms that are killed by normal atmospheric concentrations of oxygen.

facts.text: Tolerance varies: some survive up to 8% oxygen, others lose viability above 0.5%; facultative anaerobes can use oxygen but survive without it.
Oxygen harms them through reactive oxygen species, which aerobes detoxify with enzymes that obligate anaerobes make in small amounts or not at all.
They gain energy by anaerobic respiration, using acceptors such as sulfate, nitrate, iron or manganese, or by fermentation, both yielding less ATP than aerobic respiration.
They live in oxygen-free places including deep soil sediments, landfills and still waters; some Mycobacterium, Streptomyces and Rhodococcus species are soil examples.

definition.text: A chemical species that takes up electrons transferred to it from another compound, and so acts as an oxidizing agent.

facts.text: Its electron-accepting power is measured by its redox potential.
In biology the terminal electron acceptor is the last compound to receive an electron in an electron transport chain, such as oxygen in aerobic respiration.
All organisms get energy by moving electrons from a donor to an acceptor, but the terminal acceptors they use vary widely.
The herbicide paraquat is toxic because it acts as a potent electron acceptor, taking electrons from photosynthesis and passing them to oxygen to form reactive oxygen species.

definition.text: A chemical species that transfers electrons to another compound, acting as a reducing agent that is itself oxidized.

facts.text: In biology, electron donors release electrons during respiration, releasing energy; microbes capture it as electrons pass along a transport chain to an acceptor.
Soil organic matter, petroleum hydrocarbons, less chlorinated solvents such as vinyl chloride and reduced inorganic compounds can all act as electron donors.
These reactions drive natural biodegradation of organic contaminants, a major part of monitored natural attenuation at contaminated sites.

definition.text: The hypothetical charge an atom would carry if all its bonds were fully ionic, describing how far it has been oxidized.

facts.text: A rise in oxidation state is oxidation and a fall is reduction; the two always occur in pairs in redox reactions.
Pure elements have an oxidation state of zero, and oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule sum to zero.
Stock nomenclature writes it as a Roman numeral after the element, as in iron(III) oxide.
It can be an average fraction, such as 8/3 for iron in magnetite, Fe3O4.

definition.text: The reference redox electrode that sets the zero of the thermodynamic scale of oxidation–reduction potentials.

facts.text: Its standard electrode potential is declared to be zero volts at any temperature, though its absolute potential is estimated at 4.44 ± 0.02 V at 25 °C.
The potentials of all other electrodes are compared with it at the same temperature.
Soil redox potential, Eh, is the potential of a platinum electrode measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode.
It is a theoretical ideal-solution standard, replacing the older normal hydrogen electrode of platinum in 1 N acid with bubbling hydrogen.

definition.text: A plot of the thermodynamically stable phases of an aqueous system against redox potential (Eh or pe) and pH.

facts.text: Lines mark the 50/50 boundaries between the predominant dissolved species or solid phases.
Like a phase diagram it assumes equilibrium and says nothing about reaction rates.
Water is stable only between two parallel lines, EH = −0.05916 pH and EH = 1.229 V − 0.05916 pH; outside them it is reduced to hydrogen or oxidized to oxygen.
The diagrams are used in corrosion, geochemistry and environmental science, and are named after the Belgian engineer Marcel Pourbaix (1904–1998).

definition.text: The dynamic equilibrium between a solid compound and a solution of that compound, with dissolution and precipitation going on at equal rates.

facts.text: Each solubility equilibrium has a temperature-dependent solubility product that works like an equilibrium constant.
A solution at equilibrium with undissolved solid is saturated; one holding more solute than its solubility is supersaturated and can precipitate.
Strictly the constant is a quotient of activities, but it is usually converted to a quotient of concentrations.
Acid rain leaching aluminium from rocks and soil is dissolution with reaction: aluminosilicates react with the acid to give soluble Al3+.

definition.text: A soil formed under wetland conditions, waterlogged for long enough to shape its development.

facts.text: The 1938 USDA taxonomy listed hydromorphic soils as an intrazonal group, with gley soils, saturated and airless so their iron is reduced, as one sub-type.
Plinthosols form by the accumulation of iron under hydromorphic conditions.
Gypcretes can form in hydromorphic soils, among other settings.
Hydromorphic soils can have little plant-available zinc because of strong zinc sorption.

title: Electron activity (pe)

definition.text: A dimensionless measure of redox potential, defined as the negative logarithm of electron activity by analogy with pH.

facts.text: Environmental chemists often use pe instead of Eh because it works directly on a logarithmic scale; at 25 °C, pe = Eh/0.05916 = 16.903 × Eh.
Environmental pe values run from −12 to +25, because beyond these water itself is reduced or oxidized.
Along with pH, Eh or pe is a master variable in soils that both controls and is governed by chemical and biological reactions.
Redox potential and pH together constrain the solubility of manganese in soils.

notes: Phrase concept; the fullest treatment is Pourbaix diagram § Concept of pe in environmental chemistry.

definition.text: The formation of a solid, the precipitate, from a liquid solution.

facts.text: Compounds precipitate when their concentration exceeds solubility, that is, when the solution is supersaturated; precipitation is faster from strongly supersaturated solutions.
Supersaturation can arise from temperature change, solvent evaporation or mixing of solvents.
Without enough attractive force to aggregate the particles, they stay suspended as a colloid instead of settling.
Ageing a fresh precipitate in its solution gives purer, larger recrystallized particles, through Ostwald ripening.

definition.text: A measure of the effective concentration of a species in a mixture, so that its chemical potential in a real solution depends on activity as it would on concentration in an ideal one.

facts.text: Activity is dimensionless; pure solids and liquids take a = 1, and it depends on temperature, pressure, composition and the chosen standard state.
Equilibrium constants should be defined by activities but are often defined by concentrations in practice.
The activity coefficient links activity to a measured concentration; near 1, the substance behaves almost ideally.

The activity of a single ion such as Ca2+ cannot be measured, since cations cannot be added without anions; the mean ionic coefficient is measurable and predicted by Debye-Hückel theory in dilute systems.
For water as solvent, water activity is the equilibrated relative humidity.
